newsitem.title: KENYA: Amnesty condemns Burundi executions of six men.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty condemns Burundi executions of six men.

text.p: The international human rights group Amnesty International on Friday condemned Burundi's execution of six men on Thursday after trials it said were "blatantly unfair."
Burundian authorities said they carried out the executions in Bujumbura's central prison of the six men accused of playing a leading role in 1993 inter-ethnic massacres.

The six, three Hutus, two Tutsis and one ethnic Twa, included the former headmaster of Kibimba school, Gitega province, Firmat Niyonkenguruka, accused of burning 70 pupils to death in his schoolroom, according to a statement by the ministry of justice.
Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya, who took power in a coup one year ago, has started a trial of those suspected of involvement in the October 1993 coup attempt and killings.
But the London-based human rights group said the executed people had not received a fair trial and had no legal representation as required by international law.
"These are the first executions since 1981, and are all the more outrageous as they took place after blantantly unfair trials," said an Amnesty statement faxed to Reuters.
Amnesty said it had information that up to 130 other people, also convicted after unfair trials, may face imminent execution.

"Amnesty is appealing to Major Buyoya to grant clemency to all others under sentence of death and to allow for their sentences and convictions to be reviewed by a truly impartial judicial body," said Amnesty.
Amnesty also slammed the ruling military junta in the tiny tea and coffee-growing central African nation for demanding that the United Nations replace its human rights envoy Paulo Sergio Pinheiro.
"By denying Paulo Sergio Pinheiro access to the country, the government is trying to avoid international scrutiny of the very serious human rights situation which exists there," Amnesty added.

U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut said on Friday the United Nations had rejected a demand by Burundi's foreign minister Luc Rukingama for Pinheiro, assigned to the job for the past two years, to be replaced.
"We will continue to press for our special rapporteurs to be in a position to visit the countries they have been appointed to monitor," Gastaut told a news briefing.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has given in to demands by Laurent Kabila, leader of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for the replacement of Chilean Roberto Garreton as special U.N. rapporteur probing alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees by Kabila's rebels in the former Zaire.
Garreton angered the Congo ruler by releasing two critical reports of massacres by his followers based on eyewitnesses. Rights groups warned his replacement would set a precedent.
Rukingama has accused Pinheiro, a leading Brazilian human rights authority, of producing slanted reports based on unproven allegations, diplomats said.
More than 150,000 people have died in ethnic violence since 1993 after soldiers from the Tutsi-dominated army assasinated the country's first freely-elected president, Melchior Ndadaye, a Hutu.
Burundi is at war between the Tutsi army and Hutu rebels fighting for a greater political stake in the country.

More than 200,000 civilians have been ordered into camps guarded by troops since the army grabbed power in a coup last year. The military says the camps protect people against attacks by ethnic Hutu rebels.
